name: Developer Professional
desc: 60 random questions from a 100-question CCDVP bank: production operations of Claude systems at scale - reliability, observability, incident diagnosis, evaluation engineering, cost and latency, runtime security and coding-agent fleets - weighted to the exam's eight-domain blueprint.

blueprint.label: Production Integration, Reliability, and Knowledge Grounding
Agent Fleet Operations for Software Delivery
Cost and Latency Optimization at Scale

questions.q: A Managed Agents session hands a market report to four subagents and tells each to write its section to report.md. Every thread finishes cleanly, yet the file holds only one section. The team had assumed that context isolation would keep the subagents' work apart. What fixes it?
options: Give each subagent its own output path and have the coordinating agent read and merge the four files after every thread is idle
Turn off inline agents so only predefined subagents run, since each predefined agent is given its own separate sandbox and filesystem
Copy the full section plan into every subagent's prompt so each thread knows which part of report.md the others are writing at the same time
Raise the session budget so each subagent can retry its write until it finds its own section present in the shared file
questions.explain: Subagents get their own session thread, which isolates conversation context, but they share one sandbox and filesystem. Four threads writing the same path is a plain write race. Separate output paths plus a merge step by the coordinator removes the race. Predefined agents are the near-miss: they bring their own model, prompt and tools, but still share the session's sandbox. Telling each thread about the others does not serialise writes, and retry-until-present only reshuffles which writer wins.
questions.constraint: context is isolated per thread, but the sandbox and filesystem are shared
breaks: predefined agents still share the session's sandbox and filesystem
awareness of other sections does not stop concurrent writes to one file
retrying a racy write just changes which thread overwrites the others
questions.chapter: How does a lead agent delegate to other agents?

questions.q: An Agent SDK service runs on autoscaled pods that are recycled about every hour. Refunds above a threshold need a finance manager's approval, which can take a day, and today the canUseTool callback simply waits for it. Pending approvals are lost whenever a pod is recycled. Which design keeps the approval gate and survives recycling?
options: Keep waiting in canUseTool but raise the pods' termination grace period to 24 hours so a pending approval survives a routine recycle of its pod
Return a defer decision from a PreToolUse hook, persist the session to a shared session store, and resume it on any pod once approved
Have the model tell the customer the refund is pending and re-ask for approval in the next user turn when the customer replies to the pending message
Run refunds in bypassPermissions mode and have finance review each one from the audit log within a day of it being issued
questions.explain: The SDK documents this exact case: when a person may take longer than the process can stay up, a PreToolUse hook returns defer so the process can exit and resume later from the persisted session. A shared SessionStore lets any pod pick it up. A 24-hour grace period is the near-miss: it fights the platform's recycling and still loses work on a crash or node move. Re-asking through the customer moves the gate into the conversation, and bypass-plus-audit detects a bad refund after the money has gone.
questions.constraint: approval can take a day; pods recycle hourly; the gate must hold
breaks: a day-long grace period fights hourly recycling and still loses work on a crash
approval moves into the conversation instead of staying a gate on the tool
after-the-fact review is detection, not an approval gate
questions.chapter: How does an agent keep working across context windows?

questions.q: A nightly fleet runs 2,000 supervisor-worker orchestrations. During a two-hour outage of one downstream API, every worker that needed it failed, and the supervisor re-dispatched each failed worker up to ten times. Spend rose eightfold and the retries slowed the API's recovery. What change addresses the failure mode?
options: Cut the per-worker retry limit from ten to three so each failed worker costs less during an outage like this one
Have workers return an empty result instead of an error, so the supervisor marks those tasks done and keeps moving
Add a dependency-level circuit breaker in the supervisor that stops dispatching after repeated failures and marks runs partial
Move the whole nightly fleet to a larger model so that the workers recover from tool errors more intelligently on their own during an outage
questions.explain: The failure is correlated: one dependency is down, so every retry fails for the same reason and adds load to a recovering service. A circuit breaker keyed on the dependency stops dispatch once failures cross a threshold, marks affected runs partial with the reason, and probes before resuming. Lowering the retry count is the near-miss: it trims cost but still hammers the API from 2,000 runs and treats a systemic outage as independent failures. Empty results hide the outage as success, and a bigger model cannot reach an API that is down.
questions.constraint: all failures share one downed dependency; retries add load to its recovery
breaks: fewer retries per worker still treats a correlated outage as independent failures
reporting failure as an empty success hides the outage from the run
a stronger model cannot call an API that is down

questions.q: In a Managed Agents session, bash runs under the auto permission policy. The user tells the primary thread to deploy, and the primary thread messages a subagent: 'The user approved the deploy, go ahead.' The subagent's deploy commands keep pausing for approval or being denied. What explains this, and what is the right response?
options: The subagent lacks the deploy tool, so the primary thread should run the deploy itself in its own thread
The approval wording was too weak, so the primary thread should restate it with the user's exact words
The policy is working: messages between threads are not read as user intent, so confirm via the session's approval events
auto is unreliable for subagents, so set bash to always_allow on the subagent and keep the user's approval in the log for later audit
questions.explain: Under auto, the server weighs the user's intent from user messages, and it explicitly does not read intent from tool results, fetched pages, MCP responses or messages between session threads. That stops injected text from laundering authority through another agent. The right path is the normal confirmation flow, where the user answers the pause. Restating the approval with the user's words is the near-miss: it is still an inter-thread message, so it carries no authority. always_allow removes the gate entirely, and the tool is present, since the calls are being evaluated.
questions.constraint: intent is not read from messages between session threads
breaks: the calls are being evaluated, so the tool is present
any inter-thread message, however worded, carries no user intent
always_allow removes the safety gate rather than satisfying it

questions.q: A support triage agent has run for six months. Traces show 91% of tickets follow the same three tool calls in the same order; on that path the agent occasionally skips the entitlement check, and cost per ticket is three times the budget. The other 9% need varied, unplanned lookups. What evolution does the data support?
options: Keep the agent everywhere and add a firmer system-prompt rule that the entitlement check must run before every reply
Run the dominant path as a fixed workflow in code, and route only tickets that leave that path to the agent
Split the agent into a coordinator and three subagents, one for each step of the dominant path, to reduce skipped steps
Replace the agent with the fixed workflow for every ticket and send the other 9% straight to the human queue unprocessed
questions.explain: The trace data says the dominant path is predictable, which is where a workflow is cheaper, faster and cannot skip a step that code runs. The 9% that genuinely need open-ended lookups keep the agent. A firmer prompt is the near-miss: it might cut skips but cannot guarantee the check runs and leaves cost where it is. Subagents add coordination cost to a fixed path, and sending all non-standard tickets to humans throws away automation where the agent earns its cost.
questions.constraint: 91% follow one fixed path with skipped steps and high cost; 9% genuinely vary
breaks: a prompt rule cannot guarantee the check and leaves cost unchanged
multi-agent overhead on a fixed path raises cost further
drops automation for the cases where an agent is actually needed

questions.q: Nine product teams each hand-rolled an agent loop on the Messages API, and postmortems keep tracing back to homegrown handling of tool results, retries and transcripts. Six teams have no need to run the loop on their own infrastructure. Three must run it in-process inside existing services that own custom local tools. What harness standard should the platform group set?
options: Managed Agents for the six teams, and the Agent SDK for the three that must run the loop in-process with their own tools
A platform-owned loop library on the raw Messages API that all nine teams must adopt, so retries and transcripts are written once
Raw Messages API loops for all nine teams, governed by a shared checklist of tool-result, retry and transcript rules
A multi-agent framework for all nine teams, so that every product gets a coordinator with specialist subagents by default
questions.explain: The postmortems point at reinvented harness code, so the fix is to stop writing it. Teams that need not host the loop can use Managed Agents, which runs the loop for them; teams that must run it in their own process use the Agent SDK, a maintained harness they host. A platform-owned library is the near-miss: it reduces duplication but re-creates the same harness in-house, and the six teams do not need to own a loop at all. A checklist keeps nine implementations, and a multi-agent default adds cost no requirement asked for.
questions.constraint: six teams need not host the loop; three must run it in-process
breaks: rebuilds a harness in-house that maintained options already provide
keeps nine separate loop implementations, the source of the incidents
adds multi-agent cost that no stated requirement calls for
questions.chapter: What are Managed Agents, and how do you build one?

questions.q: An Agent SDK service runs on an autoscaled group. Users report that resuming yesterday's agent session fails about a third of the time with 'session not found', always after a scale-down. Transcripts are stored with the SDK defaults. What change fixes resume?
options: Enable sticky sessions on the load balancer so that each user returns to the pod that created their session
Raise the pods' memory and disk limits so that transcripts are kept for longer before the files are rotated away
Mirror transcripts to a shared backend through a session store adapter, so any pod can load and resume them
Rebuild each session by resending yesterday's messages from the application database as a new conversation
questions.explain: By default transcripts are JSONL files on the pod's local disk, and that state does not survive a scale-down or a move to another node. A SessionStore adapter mirrors transcripts to shared storage so any replica can resume them. Sticky sessions are the near-miss: they help while the pod lives, but the failures happen exactly when the pod is removed. Bigger disks do not outlive the pod, and replaying messages as a new conversation loses the session's tool state and identity.
questions.constraint: failures follow scale-down; transcripts live on local pod disk
breaks: the pod holding the transcript is the one that scale-down removes
local disk does not outlive the pod, however large it is
a replayed conversation is a new session without the original tool state

questions.q: After adding a SessionStore backed by object storage, a team can see a session's transcript in the bucket, yet a worker on another host still fails to resume it. The original run used /srv/agents/tenant-42 as its working directory; the new worker starts every resume from /app. What is the cause?
options: Object storage is eventually consistent, so the worker must wait several minutes before the transcript is readable by other hosts
The store's load method returns entries in the wrong order, so the SDK rejects the transcript as corrupt on resume from another host
Session IDs are scoped to one host, so a new session must be created and seeded with the stored transcript
Store keys include an encoding of the working directory, so resume must run from a directory matching the original
questions.explain: A session's key includes projectKey, which encodes the working directory, so resuming from a different directory looks up a different key. Resume from a working directory that matches the original run, or set the project directory name explicitly where the SDK allows it. Eventual consistency is the near-miss: plausible for object stores, but the transcript is already visible and the failure is deterministic. Nothing points to ordering, and sessions are not host-bound once a shared store exists.
questions.constraint: the transcript is in the store; the resuming worker uses a different working directory
breaks: the transcript is already visible, and the failure is deterministic, not a delay
no evidence of ordering problems; the key lookup itself misses
a shared store exists precisely so other hosts can resume

questions.q: A dashboard follows long-running Managed Agents sessions over a live event stream. When the dashboard's connection drops and it reconnects, operators see either gaps in the timeline or the same tool calls shown twice. How should the client reconnect?
options: Tail the live stream immediately on reconnect, then backfill only the events whose timestamps fall inside the gap in the timeline
List the session's event history to collect seen event IDs, then tail the live stream and skip events already seen
Open two live streams in parallel so that one stays connected whenever the other drops
Recreate the session from its agent configuration on every reconnect so the stream starts from a clean state
questions.explain: Sessions persist their event history, so the documented pattern is to list history first, seed a set of seen event IDs, then tail live and skip anything already returned. Deduplicating by ID removes both gaps and doubles. Tail-then-backfill by timestamp is the near-miss: it races, because events can arrive between the two calls, and timestamp windows are not a dedup key. Twin streams double every event, and recreating the session throws away its state.
questions.constraint: the client needs no gaps and no duplicates after a reconnect
breaks: timestamp backfill races the live tail and has no dedup key
two streams duplicate every event without fixing reconnect gaps
recreating the session discards the work in progress
questions.chapter: What are Managed Agents, and how do you build one?

questions.q: A research agent keeps one Claude Opus 5.5 conversation running for weeks, with heavy prompt caching. Leadership wants it on a newer model now, and an engineer proposes changing the model ID on the next turn of the live conversation. The agent's quality matters more than the date of the switch. What approach fits?
options: Change the model ID on the next turn of the live conversation, since the history carries everything the new model needs to continue the work
Alternate the two models turn by turn for a week so the new one gradually adapts to the conversation before taking over
Finish the current task on the pinned model, run the agent's evals on the new one, then start it in a new session from a state checkpoint
Keep the conversation on Opus 5.5 indefinitely, because any model change would break the agent's reasoning beyond repair
questions.explain: Moving a live conversation to another model drops Opus 5.5's thinking blocks, and the cache is per-model, so the next turn pays to reprocess the whole history. Switching at a task boundary, after evals on the new model, into a fresh session seeded from a structured checkpoint keeps quality controlled. Changing the ID mid-conversation is the near-miss: the history does carry over, but the reasoning state and cache do not. Alternating models doubles cache misses, and refusing to migrate is not required.
questions.constraint: quality matters more than timing; thinking blocks and cache do not cross models
breaks: the switch drops thinking blocks and misses the per-model cache
alternating models misses the cache on every turn and adapts nothing
migration is possible at a task boundary; it need not be avoided
questions.chapter: How does an agent keep working across context windows?

questions.q: An Agent SDK job enables file checkpointing so it can roll a repository back when a task fails review. After one failed task, rewindFiles() restored the files Claude edited with Edit, but several config files the agent changed with sed -i stayed modified. How should the job guarantee a clean rollback?
options: Snapshot the working tree with git before each task and restore from that snapshot, since rewind covers only tool edits
Call rewindFiles() a second time after the first rewind completes so it catches the remaining modified files
Create checkpoints more often, at every tool call rather than every turn, so the Bash changes are also captured in the backups
Enable checkpointing for subagents as well, because the sed commands were most likely run inside a subagent
questions.explain: File checkpointing tracks Write, Edit and NotebookEdit; it does not undo what a Bash command such as sed -i did to a file the main conversation had not already edited with a tool. A git snapshot (or a disposable worktree) per task covers every change regardless of how it was made. Checkpointing more often is the near-miss: the gap is which changes are tracked, not how frequently. A second rewind restores nothing new, and the stem gives no sign that subagents ran the commands.
questions.constraint: rewind covers tool edits, not changes made by Bash commands
breaks: a second rewind has no record of the Bash changes to restore
frequency is not the gap; Bash changes are not tracked at all
nothing indicates a subagent ran the sed commands
questions.chapter: How does an agent keep working across context windows?

questions.q: Sixty cached turns into a long agentic session, compliance requires a new rule: every SQL statement from now on must be parameterised. Engineers appended the rule to the top-level system prompt, and the next request reprocessed the whole history at full price. The rule must carry system-level authority. What should they have done?
options: Restart the session with the new system prompt and a short summary of the history, so the cache can be rebuilt from scratch
Send the rule in the next user message, prefixed with 'SYSTEM:', so the history before it stays byte-identical
Append a mid-conversation system message carrying the rule at the current point in the history
Insert the rule at the very top of the system prompt and then move the cache breakpoint further down the history
questions.explain: A message with role system can be appended at the point where an instruction starts to apply, so everything before it stays the same and the cached prefix still matches, while the rule keeps system authority. The 'SYSTEM:' user message is the near-miss: it does preserve the cache, but it is user-turn text that the model weighs as user content, and anyone can type that prefix. Restarting throws away history and cache, and any edit near the top of the system prompt changes the prefix hash however the breakpoint moves.
questions.constraint: the rule needs system authority and the cached history must still hit
breaks: a restart discards both the cache and the session's detail
keeps the cache, but a user turn does not carry system authority
any change to the top-level system prompt invalidates the cache
questions.chapter: How does an agent keep working across context windows?

questions.q: A coding agent needs a migrate_database tool only in its final phase, and the team does not want the model to see it earlier. Today they add the tool to the tools array when that phase begins, and that turn's cache hit rate drops to zero across a long conversation. Which approach keeps the cache?
options: Add the tool at the start, and tell the model in the system prompt not to call it until the final phase
Declare the tool up front with defer_loading set, then surface it later with a tool_addition in a system message
Append the new tool to the end of the tools array instead of the start, so that the earlier entries stay the same
Start a second conversation for the final phase that has the tool, and copy the earlier transcript into it as text
questions.explain: The tools array sits ahead of the system prompt in the hashed prefix, so any edit to it invalidates the cache for the whole conversation, wherever in the array the change sits. Declaring the tool from the first request with defer_loading keeps it out of the model's view, and a tool_addition block in a later system message surfaces it without changing the prefix. Offering it from the start with a 'not yet' instruction keeps the cache but exposes the tool early. A new conversation pays to process the history again.
questions.constraint: the tool must stay hidden until the final phase without breaking the cache
breaks: keeps the cache but exposes the tool to the model early
any edit to the tools array invalidates the whole cache, wherever it sits
a new conversation reprocesses the full history at full price
questions.chapter: How does Claude use tools, MCP and web search?

questions.q: An agent enables server-side tool result clearing with a low trigger. Context stays small, but input cost went up: every few turns a small amount is cleared and the next request writes a fresh cache entry for most of the prompt. What tuning addresses this?
options: Turn clearing off and rely on the model's context window, since clearing costs more than it saves on long runs
Clear on every turn instead, so that each cache write stays as small as possible
Set a minimum amount to clear each time, so each invalidation frees enough tokens to pay for the cache rewrite
Move the cache breakpoint to the first user turn so that clearing older tool results leaves cached content alone
questions.explain: Clearing tool results invalidates the cached prefix from the cleared point, so frequent small clears turn into frequent cache rewrites. The clear_at_least parameter makes each clearing remove enough tokens to be worth the invalidation, and a higher trigger helps too. Turning clearing off is the near-miss: it removes the rewrites but lets context grow without limit, which clearing exists to stop. Clearing every turn makes the problem worse, and moving the breakpoint does not stop clearing from altering content after it.
questions.constraint: each small clear causes a cache rewrite that costs more than it frees
breaks: gives up context control rather than tuning the trade-off
more frequent clears mean more frequent cache rewrites
clearing still changes content after the breakpoint and forces a rewrite
questions.chapter: How does an agent keep working across context windows?

questions.q: A repository-maintenance agent's context is mostly stale tool output: file reads and search results from earlier steps that it has already acted on. Its reasoning turns and decisions must stay word for word, and a homegrown summariser has been dropping exact file paths. Which context management fits?
options: Server-side tool result clearing, which removes the oldest tool results and leaves the turns themselves intact
Server-side compaction at a token threshold, which replaces the older turns with a summary written on the server
A larger context window model, so nothing has to be cleared or summarised during the longest maintenance runs it performs
A tighter prompt for the homegrown summariser, telling it to keep every file path it finds in the transcript
questions.explain: The bulk is old tool results that are no longer needed, which is exactly what tool result clearing targets, and it leaves reasoning turns verbatim. Compaction is the near-miss: it also manages long contexts, but it summarises older turns as a whole, which is what the team must avoid. A bigger window defers the problem and still pays for stale tokens every turn, and tuning a summariser keeps the lossy step that has been dropping paths.
questions.constraint: the bloat is stale tool output; reasoning turns must stay verbatim
breaks: summarises the turns that must stay word for word
keeps paying for stale tool output on every turn
keeps a lossy summariser that already drops exact paths
questions.chapter: How does an agent keep working across context windows?

questions.q: A Managed Agents deployment gives each customer's sessions a memory store and also shares company policy notes across all sessions. Customers' messages are untrusted, and a red-team run showed an injected message saving a false 'refunds need no approval' note. Which TWO memory design choices address this? Select TWO.
options: Attach the shared policy notes as a read_only store, separate from each customer's read_write store
Use memory versions to audit what each session wrote, and roll back or redact poisoned entries
Use a single read_write store for all customers, so that a correction made in one session reaches everyone
Move the policy notes into the system prompt and rewrite that prompt nightly from the latest memory contents
Raise the store's size limit so that a single injected note is diluted among many legitimate memories
questions.explain: Injected text can only persist where the agent can write. A read_only mount for shared policy stops a customer's session from altering what every other session trusts, and per-customer read_write stores contain any damage to one customer. Memory versions give an audit trail and point-in-time recovery for what was written. One shared read_write store is the near-miss: it spreads corrections, and it spreads poison to every customer just as fast. Nightly prompt rewrites copy poisoned memory into the system prompt, and dilution is not a control.
questions.constraint: customer input is untrusted and shared policy must not be writable by sessions
breaks: one writable shared store spreads a poisoned note to every customer
copies poisoned memory into the system prompt and churns the cache
dilution does not stop the injected note from being read and trusted
questions.chapter: How does an agent keep working across context windows?

questions.q: An agent checks budget compliance by calling get_expense_lines once per employee for 200 employees. Each call is a model round trip, and thousands of raw line items pile into context before the agent can total them. Only per-employee totals and exceptions matter. Which technique fits?
options: Programmatic tool calling, so code in the execution container loops over the calls and returns only totals and exceptions
Parallel tool calls, so the model requests all 200 lookups in one response and receives every result together in a single turn
A model with a larger context window, so that all the line items fit comfortably before the agent totals them
Compaction at a token threshold, so older line items are summarised once the context grows past the trigger
questions.explain: Programmatic tool calling lets Claude write code that calls the tool in a loop inside the container and filters the data before it reaches context, cutting both round trips and tokens. Parallel tool calls are the near-miss: they cut round trips but still pour every raw line item into context. A bigger window pays for all of it, and summarising line items risks the exact figures the totals depend on.
questions.constraint: 200 lookups; only totals and exceptions are needed in context
breaks: fewer round trips, but every raw line item still lands in context
pays to hold thousands of raw items the task does not need
summarising line items risks losing the exact figures the totals need

questions.q: A product launch pushed traffic from near zero to full volume within two minutes. Many requests returned 429 although dashboards showed the organisation well under its ITPM and OTPM limits, and the 429s cleared on their own over the next half hour. What should the team change before the next launch?
options: Request a higher usage tier before the launch, because the tier's ITPM and OTPM limits were clearly too low for the peak
Retry every 429 immediately in a tight loop, since capacity under the published limits will free up within seconds
Ramp traffic up in steps ahead of the launch and honour retry-after with jittered backoff and a queue in front
Fail over to a second region on the first 429 and keep traffic there for the rest of the launch window
questions.explain: A 429 while under ITPM and OTPM after a sharp increase is a ramp limit: the allowed growth is based on recent per-minute usage plus a step, and it comes back down after quiet periods. Ramping traffic up beforehand, plus backoff and a queue, stays inside it. A higher tier is the near-miss: it raises the steady-state limits, but the dashboards show those were not the binding constraint. Tight-loop retries make the burst worse, and blind regional failover is not what the 429 signals.
questions.constraint: 429s while under ITPM and OTPM right after a sharp increase
breaks: the steady-state limits were not binding; the growth rate was
tight-loop retries add to the burst that triggered the limit
the 429 reflects growth rate, not a regional fault

questions.domain: Production Integration, Reliability, and Knowledge Grounding
questions.q: On the last evening of the month, a pipeline's retry queue fills with 429s that never succeed, even after backing off for an hour. Unlike the usual rate-limit 429s, these responses carry no retry-after header. What should the retry layer do differently?
options: Read the error code to tell a spend-cap 429 from a rate limit, stop retrying those, and alert someone to act on the cap
Back off longer, up to a full day, because a missing retry-after header means the reset time is simply further away than usual
Spread the queued retries evenly across all workspaces so no single workspace keeps hitting its own limit
Raise the SDK's retry count so each request has more chances to succeed before it is finally dropped
questions.explain: A spend-cap 429 has no retry-after and keeps failing until access resumes, and the documented way to tell it from a rate limit in code is the error code. Retrying is pointless; someone has to raise the cap or wait, so the retry layer should stop and alert. Longer backoff is the near-miss: it fits the usual rate-limit pattern, but here no amount of waiting inside the month helps and the queue keeps growing. Shuffling workspaces or adding retries treats a billing stop as congestion.
questions.constraint: 429s with no retry-after that keep failing at month end
breaks: a spend-cap 429 keeps failing until access resumes; waiting does not fix it
a spend cap is not a per-workspace congestion problem
more retries just keep failing against the cap

questions.domain: Production Integration, Reliability, and Knowledge Grounding
questions.q: A team enabled server-side fallback with fallbacks set to 'default' on every request, expecting it to protect them from model incidents. During an overload event, 529 errors reached users and no request was served by another model. What should they add?
options: Name up to three fallback models explicitly instead of 'default', so that overloads route to models they have qualified in advance
Their own retry with backoff and a cross-model or cross-region fallback for overload and server errors, alongside fallbacks
Nothing in code; raise a support case, because server-side fallback is meant to catch 529 overload errors as well
Disable server-side fallback entirely, because it delayed the 529 responses that the client should have seen sooner
questions.explain: Server-side fallback is triggered only by a safety classifier decline; a rate limit, overload or server error is returned as-is. Overload resilience needs the team's own retry, backoff and model or region fallback. Naming explicit fallback models is the near-miss: it changes which model serves a refused request, but it still fires only on refusals, so 529s pass straight through. A support case misreads the feature, and disabling fallback removes refusal handling without adding overload handling.
questions.constraint: fallbacks fire only on safety declines; the incident was 529 overloads
breaks: named fallbacks still trigger only on refusals, not overloads
the feature is documented to return overloads as-is
removes refusal handling and adds no overload handling
questions.course: Production Integration, Reliability, and Knowledge Grounding
questions.chapter: Why can you get a 429 when you're under your limit?

questions.domain: Production Integration, Reliability, and Knowledge Grounding
questions.q: A cost cascade sends easy requests to Claude Haiku 5.5 and harder ones to Claude Opus 5.5, and every request sets fallbacks to 'default'. Refused requests on the Opus path are retried on another model as expected, but refused requests on the Haiku path come back to users as refusals. What fixes the Haiku path?
options: Route every request to Opus 5.5 so that all traffic benefits from server-side fallback, accepting the higher cost
Retry each Haiku refusal on Haiku with a lower effort setting, since a lighter pass is less likely to trip the classifier a second time
Raise the Haiku requests' max_tokens so the response has room to complete instead of stopping as a refusal
Handle Haiku refusals with the SDK middleware or a manual retry to a fallback model, since server-side fallback is absent there
questions.explain: Claude Haiku 5.5 has neither server-side fallback nor fallback credit, so the documented path for it is client-side: the SDK middleware or a manual retry. That keeps the cascade's economics and restores fallback on the cheap path. Routing everything to Opus is the near-miss: it does give every request server-side fallback, but it throws away the cascade the team built for cost. Lower effort does not change a classifier decision, and a refusal is not a length stop.
questions.constraint: Haiku 5.5 has no server-side fallback; the cascade exists for cost
breaks: restores fallback by abandoning the cost cascade
effort does not change a safety classifier decision
a refusal is not a length stop, so max_tokens is irrelevant
questions.course: Production Integration, Reliability, and Knowledge Grounding
questions.chapter: Why can you get a 429 when you're under your limit?

questions.domain: Production Integration, Reliability, and Knowledge Grounding
questions.q: A streaming chat UI occasionally shows answers that stop mid-sentence with no error. Logs show the HTTP status was 200 each time, and the client's retry wrapper only acts on non-2xx statuses. Server-sent events in those streams end with an error event of type overloaded_error. What should change?
options: Raise max_tokens on streaming requests, since the answers stop early because they run out of output budget
Rely on the SDK to retry these failures automatically, and simply surface its final error to the user if all retries fail
Switch the chat UI to non-streaming requests so that every failure surfaces as an HTTP status the wrapper understands
Handle error events inside the stream: discard the partial answer, then retry with backoff or show a clear failure
questions.explain: Errors can arrive as SSE error events after a 200, so a status-based wrapper never sees them, and the SDK does not retry an error inside a stream. The client must watch for error events, drop the partial output and retry or report. Moving to non-streaming is the near-miss: it does make failures visible as statuses, but it gives up streaming's first-token latency and long-request handling to work around a client bug. max_tokens is not the cause, and the SDK will not retry these for you.
questions.constraint: errors arrive as events inside a 200 stream; the SDK does not retry them
breaks: the stream ended with an error event, not a length stop
the SDK does not retry an error inside a stream
fixes visibility by giving up streaming instead of handling events

questions.domain: Production Integration, Reliability, and Knowledge Grounding
questions.q: During a partial outage, about 40% of requests return 529. Each of 30 pods wraps its SDK client call in its own five-attempt retry loop with a fixed one-second delay, and load on the API climbs as the incident goes on. The SDK is used with default settings. What change best restores stability?
options: Shorten the outer loop's fixed delay to 200 ms, so each request finishes its five attempts sooner and frees capacity for requests on the other pods
Raise the SDK's max_retries so that the SDK, rather than the outer loop, absorbs more of the transient 529 errors
Remove the nested retry: keep one layer with jittered exponential backoff, a retry budget, and a breaker that sheds to a degraded mode
Add more pods so that the extra retry traffic is spread across more workers and each pod handles fewer requests
questions.explain: The SDK already retries a failed request up to two times by default, so each outer attempt is really up to three calls: five outer attempts make as many as fifteen calls per request, all on a fixed schedule. One retry layer with jittered backoff, a budget, and a breaker that falls back to cached or queued responses cuts the amplification. Raising max_retries is the near-miss: it moves retries into the SDK but, with the outer loop still there, multiplies attempts further. Shorter delays and more pods both add load to a struggling service.
questions.constraint: nested retries: an outer 5-attempt loop over an SDK that already retries
breaks: faster retries add load during the outage
with the outer loop still present, more SDK retries multiply attempts further
more pods send more retries to an overloaded API

questions.domain: Production Integration, Reliability, and Knowledge Grounding
questions.q: A capacity plan says a document Q&A service needs three times its current ITPM limit at next quarter's volume. The plan counts every input token in each request, but about 80% of input tokens are a shared document prefix read from the prompt cache. What should the team do first?
options: Request a usage tier with three times the ITPM limit now, before the volume arrives and requests begin to fail at peak
Recompute the plan on uncached input tokens, since cache reads do not count toward ITPM, and work on the hit rate
Split the traffic across three workspaces so that each one stays within the organisation's current ITPM limit
Move the shared document out of the prompt and into retrieval so fewer tokens count toward the ITPM limit at peak volume
questions.explain: The default ITPM limits count only uncached input tokens, so cache reads do not consume the limit. With an 80% hit rate, the plan overstates ITPM need several times over; recompute on uncached tokens and keep the hit rate high. Requesting a bigger tier is the near-miss: reasonable if the arithmetic were right, but it is planned on tokens that do not count. Workspaces subdivide the organisation's limit rather than adding to it, and dropping a well-cached prefix gives up the very tokens that are cheapest.
questions.constraint: 80% of input tokens are cache reads, which do not count toward ITPM
breaks: plans capacity on cached tokens that do not count toward ITPM
workspace limits subdivide the organisation's limit rather than adding to it
removes the cheapest, uncounted tokens instead of fixing the plan

questions.domain: Production Integration, Reliability, and Knowledge Grounding
questions.q: A report generator writes about 6,000 output tokens per request. It hits 429s at peak while input-token utilisation sits near 20% of ITPM. An engineer cut max_tokens from 16,000 to 8,000 to 'reserve less output capacity', and the 429 rate did not change. What is binding, and what helps?
options: Input tokens are binding after all, so the fix is to shorten the prompt template and send fewer documents per request
OTPM is binding on tokens actually generated, so pace output-heavy work on OTPM headroom or move it to batch
Requests per minute are binding, so the fix is to merge several reports into each request to cut the request count
max_tokens still reserves capacity, so it should be lowered again until it sits just above the typical output length
questions.explain: OTPM is evaluated as output tokens are produced, counting only tokens actually generated, and max_tokens does not factor in. With input at 20% and long outputs, OTPM is the binding limit; pace on output headroom or move non-urgent reports to the Batches API. Lowering max_tokens further is the near-miss: it feels like reserving less, but OTPM never counted it, and too low a value truncates reports. Input is clearly not binding, and merging reports does not reduce output tokens.
questions.constraint: input at 20% of ITPM; long outputs; cutting max_tokens changed nothing
breaks: input utilisation is low, so ITPM is not the binding limit
merging requests leaves the output tokens, and so OTPM, unchanged
max_tokens does not count toward OTPM; lowering it risks truncation

questions.domain: Production Integration, Reliability, and Knowledge Grounding
questions.q: A multi-tenant SaaS shares one organisation's rate limits across 4,000 tenants. One tenant's bulk import last week starved everyone else for an hour. An engineer proposes a separate workspace for every tenant so each gets its own limits. What is the better design?
options: A workspace per tenant for all 4,000 tenants, each set to an equal share of the organisation's ITPM and OTPM limits
A single shared queue in first-in, first-out order, so that every request waits its turn regardless of which tenant sent it or how many it has queued
Per-tenant queues with weighted fair scheduling and concurrency caps in the app, plus separate workspaces for a few large tiers
Reject any tenant's request once that tenant sends more than a fixed number of requests per minute, with no queueing
questions.explain: Fair sharing across thousands of tenants belongs in the application: per-tenant queues, weighted fair scheduling and concurrency caps stop one tenant's burst from starving others while keeping capacity usable. Workspaces can still carry lower user-configurable limits for a handful of tiers. One workspace per tenant is the near-miss: organisations have a workspace cap, workspace limits subdivide rather than add capacity, and caches are isolated per workspace. FIFO lets the bulk import fill the queue, and hard rejection with no queue drops legitimate bursts.
questions.constraint: 4,000 tenants share one organisation's limits; one tenant's burst starved the rest
breaks: exceeds the workspace cap and fragments limits and caches across 4,000 tenants
a FIFO queue lets one tenant's burst fill it and starve the others
hard rejection drops legitimate bursts instead of smoothing them

questions.domain: Production Integration, Reliability, and Knowledge Grounding
questions.q: A nightly Message Batches job sends 400,000 requests. On busy nights a few thousand results come back as expired, and the morning report is missing those documents. What should the pipeline do?
options: Resubmit only the expired and retryable errored requests in a new batch, and start large batches earlier or split them
Resubmit the entire batch whenever any result has expired, so that the morning report is built from one complete run of the job
Treat expired requests as permanent failures and leave those documents out of the report until the next night
Move the whole nightly job to synchronous requests so nothing can expire, accepting full price for every document in the nightly run
questions.explain: A request expires when the batch hits its 24-hour limit before the request was sent to the model, so it never ran and can simply be resubmitted. Resubmit just those (plus retryable errors), and start or split large batches so they finish in time. Resubmitting everything is the near-miss: it does produce one consistent run, but pays twice for hundreds of thousands of results that already succeeded. Dropping the documents loses data that only needed resubmitting, and abandoning batch gives up its discount for a few thousand stragglers.
questions.constraint: only a few thousand of 400,000 requests expired before running
breaks: pays again for the hundreds of thousands of requests that already succeeded
expired requests never ran, so they can simply be resubmitted
gives up the batch discount on all traffic to rescue a few thousand requests

questions.domain: Production Integration, Reliability, and Knowledge Grounding
questions.q: A batch of 50,000 requests shares an identical 30,000-token instruction and reference prefix, but cache read tokens are low across the results. Which TWO changes are most likely to raise the cache hit rate? Select TWO.
options: Use the 1-hour cache duration on the shared prefix, because batch processing can outlast the 5-minute default
Keep the shared prefix byte-identical in every request, with any per-document content placed after the breakpoint
Add a max_tokens: 0 request at the start of the batch so it pre-warms the cache before the rest are processed
Spread the requests across several workspaces so each workspace builds and serves its own copy of the cache in parallel
Send the batch through Priority Tier so that requests are processed in order and reuse the cache more often
questions.explain: Batches can take longer than five minutes, so the 1-hour cache duration keeps the shared prefix alive between requests, and the prefix must be byte-identical up to the breakpoint for any request to hit it. Pre-warming with max_tokens: 0 is the near-miss: it works for synchronous traffic but is not supported inside a batch, because the entry would likely expire before the follow-up runs. Spreading across workspaces makes things worse, since caches are isolated per workspace, and Priority Tier does not order or cache batch work.
questions.constraint: a long-running batch with one shared prefix and low cache reads
breaks: cache pre-warming with max_tokens: 0 is not supported inside a batch
caches are isolated per workspace, so splitting multiplies cache writes
service tier does not order batch requests or improve cache reuse

questions.domain: Production Integration, Reliability, and Knowledge Grounding
questions.q: A team adds its internal ticketing MCP server to Messages API requests through the MCP connector. The server runs on a private network reachable only from the company VPN, and every request fails to connect to it. Which change makes the integration work?
options: Pass a longer-lived OAuth token in the server's authorization_token field, so that the connection is accepted by the private server
Run an MCP client inside the application on the private network and pass the server's tools to Claude yourself
Switch the connector's transport from Streamable HTTP to SSE, which the MCP connector handles more reliably
Add the API's egress addresses to the VPN client config so that the private address resolves for the connector at request time
questions.explain: The MCP connector calls the server from Anthropic's side, so the server must be publicly exposed over HTTP. A server reachable only on a private network needs a client that runs where it can reach it: the application connects to the MCP server itself (the SDK has helpers for this) and passes the tools to Claude. A different token is the near-miss: authentication matters, but no token makes a private address reachable. Both transports need a public endpoint, and a VPN client config does not expose a private address to an external caller.
questions.constraint: the MCP server is reachable only on a private network
breaks: no token makes a private network address reachable from outside
both transports require a publicly reachable endpoint
a VPN client config does not expose a private server to an external caller

questions.domain: Production Integration, Reliability, and Knowledge Grounding
questions.q: A Messages API agent uses the MCP connector with an allowlist: default_config disables all tools and configs enables search_tickets. After the vendor renamed it to ticket_search, nothing errored, but the agent stopped searching and its grounded-answer rate fell for a week before anyone noticed. What prevents a repeat?
options: Enable all of the server's tools by default and denylist only the destructive ones, so renamed tools stay usable
Pin the vendor's MCP server to its current version so that tool names cannot change again without notice from the vendor's side
A CI contract test that compares the server's live tool list with the configured allowlist, plus an alert on tool-call rate
Ask the model in the system prompt to report whenever a tool it expects to use is missing from the tools it can see
questions.explain: When a name in configs does not exist on the server, the connector logs a warning but returns no error, so a rename silently removes the tool. A contract test that diffs the live tool inventory against the allowlist catches the change before release, and an alert on tool-call rate catches it in production. Switching to a denylist is the near-miss: renamed tools would keep working, but so would every new tool the vendor ships, unreviewed. Pinning may not be possible on a vendor server, and asking the model to notice an absence is not a reliable control.
questions.constraint: an unknown tool name in configs is ignored without an error
breaks: keeps renamed tools, but also enables every new unreviewed tool
vendor servers may not support pinning, and it does not detect drift
relying on the model to notice a missing tool is not a reliable control

questions.domain: Production Integration, Reliability, and Knowledge Grounding
questions.q: An extraction pipeline forces its record_invoice tool with tool_choice type 'tool'. In staging, switching the model to claude-opus-5-5 makes every request fail with a 400 error. The team wants guaranteed schema-valid records on the new model. What change should the migration make?
options: Keep tool_choice set to 'tool' and send an assistant prefill that opens the tool call, so the model has no other choice
Switch tool_choice to 'any', which still forces some tool call while being accepted more widely than naming one tool
Use tool_choice auto with strict tool use or structured outputs, and set effort explicitly before re-running the evals
Roll the pipeline back to the previous model permanently, because the new model cannot produce forced structured output
questions.explain: Claude Opus 5.5 rejects forced tool use (both 'any' and a named tool) with a 400, and it rejects assistant prefill too. The migration path is auto plus strict tool use or structured outputs for schema guarantees, with effort set explicitly because its default differs from the previous Opus model. 'any' is the near-miss: it looks like a softer force but is rejected the same way. Prefill is also rejected, and abandoning the migration is unnecessary when structured outputs give the guarantee.
questions.constraint: forced tool choice returns 400 on the new model; schema validity is still required
breaks: prefill is rejected on the new model, and forced tool use still fails
'any' is a forced tool choice and is rejected just like a named tool
schema guarantees are available on the new model through structured outputs

questions.domain: Production Integration, Reliability, and Knowledge Grounding
questions.q: A team updates its Managed Agents agent with a new system prompt and tool set. Their session-creation code passes the agent ID as a plain string, so the change reached every new session at once, and a regression hit all users. How should future agent changes be rolled out?
options: Pin sessions to an explicit agent version, create a small share of sessions on the new version, then widen it
Create a brand-new agent for every change and switch all session creation to the new agent ID in a single deploy
Edit the system prompt only during low-traffic hours, so that a regression affects fewer users before it is caught
Keep passing the plain agent ID but run the evals twice before each update, so regressions are less likely to ship
questions.explain: Passing the agent ID as a string creates sessions on the latest version, so every update is an instant full rollout. Pinning sessions to a specific version lets you route a canary share to the new version, compare, widen, and roll back by pinning the old version. A new agent per change is the near-miss: it isolates versions, but switching all traffic at once is the same big-bang release. Low-traffic timing and extra evals reduce exposure or likelihood, but neither gives a staged rollout or quick rollback.
questions.constraint: a plain agent ID always means the latest version for new sessions
breaks: still a single cut-over of all traffic, with no canary
smaller exposure, but no staged rollout or rollback path
more testing, but every update still reaches all sessions at once

questions.domain: Production Integration, Reliability, and Knowledge Grounding
questions.q: A support assistant's prompt is changed several times a month, and last month an edit that passed review doubled the escalation rate before anyone noticed. Which TWO practices should the release process add? Select TWO.
options: Version each prompt as a build artifact and gate its release on the regression eval suite in CI
Release to a small share of traffic first, with automatic rollback when a guard metric such as escalation rate moves
Edit the production prompt in place during quiet hours so that any regression reaches fewer users before it is caught
Move to 100% of traffic as soon as the offline evals pass, since a passing eval suite already proves there is no regression
Let each server pick a prompt version at random without logging which one served a request, to spread the risk
questions.explain: A prompt is code that changes behaviour, so it needs a versioned artifact with an eval gate before release and a progressive rollout with an automatic rollback trigger after it. Offline evals and live guard metrics catch different failures. Going to 100% once evals pass is the near-miss: the gate is necessary, but offline suites miss shifts that only real traffic shows, which is what happened here. Quiet-hour edits skip both gates, and unlogged random versions make a regression impossible to attribute.
questions.constraint: a reviewed edit still caused a live regression that went unnoticed
breaks: skips both the eval gate and the staged rollout
offline evals alone missed exactly this kind of live regression
without a logged version, a regression cannot be traced or rolled back

questions.domain: Production Integration, Reliability, and Knowledge Grounding
questions.q: A policy assistant gives wrong answers on about 6% of questions. For those, traces show the correct passage was retrieved at rank 35 of 50 candidates, but only the top 8 after reranking are sent to the model; on correct answers, the right passage is usually in the top 3. Which stage should the team fix first?
options: Generation: rewrite the answer prompt so that the model reasons more carefully over the passages it is given
Chunking: re-split all documents into much smaller chunks so that each passage is easier for the model to read and to quote
Embedding: replace the embedding model, because the right passage is not being retrieved for these questions
Ranking: tune or replace the reranker and test a wider pass-through, since the passage is found but cut before generation
questions.explain: Diagnose by stage. The correct passage is in the candidate set, so first-stage retrieval works; it is lost when reranking keeps only the top 8, so the model never sees it. Fix ranking (better reranker, wider pass-through within budget) and measure recall at the cut. Replacing the embedding model is the near-miss: it is the usual suspect for retrieval misses, but here retrieval already found the passage. Prompt changes cannot use a passage the model never received, and re-chunking changes everything without targeting the observed loss.
questions.constraint: the correct passage is retrieved at rank 35 but cut by the top-8 rerank
breaks: the model never received the passage, so prompting cannot fix it
re-chunking does not target the observed loss at the rerank cut
first-stage retrieval already finds the passage

questions.domain: Production Integration, Reliability, and Knowledge Grounding
questions.q: A contracts tool must return JSON that downstream code parses, and each extracted clause must carry a citation that auditors can trust points into the source document. Enabling both the citations feature and structured outputs on one request fails. What design meets both needs?
options: Keep structured outputs and add a quote field to the schema, telling the model to copy the clause text exactly
Keep citations on the answer and build the JSON in code from the response's citation blocks and text
Enable both features on alternate requests, so half of the documents get citations and half get valid JSON
Drop citations and have a second model check whether each quoted clause appears somewhere in the document
questions.explain: Citations cannot be used with structured outputs, because citation blocks are interleaved with text. Citations are parsed by the API and are guaranteed to point into the provided documents, so the trustworthy route is to keep them and assemble the JSON in code from the cited spans. A quote field in a strict schema is the near-miss: the JSON parses, but the quote is model-written text with no guaranteed link to the source. Alternating requests satisfies neither requirement per document, and a second model's check is probabilistic.
questions.constraint: citations and structured outputs cannot be combined; citations must be trustworthy
breaks: a model-written quote field has no guaranteed pointer into the source
no single document gets both a citation and valid JSON
replaces guaranteed pointers with a probabilistic second-model check

questions.domain: Production Integration, Reliability, and Knowledge Grounding
questions.q: A code Q&A assistant answers from an embedding index rebuilt nightly, while the repositories change hundreds of times a day. Wrong answers cluster on code changed since the last rebuild, and the latency budget is 20 seconds. Questions about the stable design docs are answered well. What should change?
options: Rebuild the code index every hour instead of nightly, so stale chunks are replaced much sooner after each change
Answer code questions with agentic search over the live repository, such as grep and file reads, keeping the index for docs
Add a disclaimer telling users that answers may not reflect today's changes to the code, without changing retrieval or the index schedule
Lower the similarity threshold so that the index returns more chunks for each code question it is asked
questions.explain: The failures are a freshness problem confined to fast-changing code. Agentic search reads the live repository at query time, so it cannot be stale, and a 20-second budget allows a few tool calls. The stable docs keep the index, where it works. Hourly rebuilds are the near-miss: they shrink the window but still serve code up to an hour out of date in a repository that changes hundreds of times a day. A disclaimer accepts wrong answers, and lower thresholds return more stale chunks.
questions.constraint: code changes constantly, the index is nightly, and the budget allows tool calls
breaks: still serves code that is up to an hour out of date
accepts the wrong answers instead of fixing retrieval
returns more chunks from the same stale index
questions.course: Production Integration, Reliability, and Knowledge Grounding
questions.chapter: How do you improve retrieval in a RAG system?

questions.domain: Production Integration, Reliability, and Knowledge Grounding
questions.q: A RAG service returns retrieved passages to Claude as plain text inside a tool result. Answers cite well in testing, but the product team wants every citation to show the source document's title and link, as web search citations do. Which change provides that?
options: Return the passages as search_result content blocks with a source and title, and enable citations
Append each passage's URL to the end of its text and tell the model to repeat that URL after every claim it makes
Ask for a sources list at the end of the answer, generated by the model from the passages it used in the reply
Merge all retrieved passages into one large text document block, so the API can number them for citations
questions.explain: Search result content blocks let Claude cite your own content the way it cites web search results, with each citation carrying the source and title you supplied. Returned from a retrieval tool, they give structured, attributable citations. Asking the model to repeat URLs is the near-miss: it often works, but the link is model-written text that can be dropped or garbled, not a citation field. A model-written sources list has the same weakness, and merging passages into one document loses each one's separate source and title.
questions.constraint: citations must carry each source's title and link like web search results
breaks: a model-repeated URL is free text, not a structured citation field
a model-written sources list can drift from what was actually used
one merged document loses each passage's separate source and title

questions.q: A team on a zero-data-retention agreement exports Claude API traces to its observability platform. Spans show timing, status and token counts but no prompts or responses, and a quality investigation needs to read the failing conversations. Engineers assume content capture is impossible under ZDR. What is accurate?
options: Content export is barred under ZDR, so the team must log prompts and responses in its own application instead
Setting OTEL_LOG_USER_PROMPTS=1 in the application's environment will add prompts and responses to the API's spans
Spans default to metadata only; Full content is available under ZDR, held in memory only until it is delivered
Prompts appear only on spans the API flags as errors, so the team should filter its platform to failed requests
questions.explain: Destinations default to Metadata only, which carries identifiers, timing, status and token counts but no prompts. Full content can be turned on, and with ZDR the API holds Messages API content only in memory until it delivers it to the destination. The 'barred under ZDR' option is the near-miss: plausible, but the docs allow Full content with ZDR. OTEL_LOG_USER_PROMPTS is a Claude Code setting, not an API destination control, and content is not limited to error spans.
questions.constraint: ZDR is in place and spans currently carry metadata only
breaks: Full content is allowed under ZDR for Messages API requests
that variable configures Claude Code telemetry, not API trace destinations
content capture is a destination setting, not tied to error spans

questions.q: A healthcare company set its OpenTelemetry destination's content mode to Full content, yet Claude API spans still arrive with metadata only. The destination shows Healthy, and the organisation has a HIPAA data-handling restriction with Anthropic. What explains this?
options: The destination's maximum content size is too small, so the content is silently trimmed down to metadata before export
With a HIPAA restriction, destinations export only metadata whatever their content mode; SDK spans are not affected
Full content takes up to 24 hours to apply after the change, so spans will include content from tomorrow onward
The observability platform strips large span attributes on ingest, so the content is dropped before it reaches its storage layer in the backend
questions.explain: For organisations with a HIPAA, FERPA or K-12 data-handling restriction, destinations export only metadata regardless of the content mode. SDK spans are not affected by that rule, so content can come from there if your own policy allows it. The size-limit option is the near-miss: a real setting, but a small limit truncates content rather than removing all of it, and this is a policy outcome. There is no 24-hour delay, and a Healthy destination with zero content points at the policy, not ingest.
questions.constraint: the organisation has a HIPAA data-handling restriction
breaks: a size limit truncates content; it does not reduce every span to metadata
no documented delay; the restriction applies whatever the mode
the export itself carries metadata only, so ingest is not the cause

questions.q: An application propagates W3C trace context to the Claude API and uses 10% head sampling. About 90% of Messages API requests have no API spans in the backend, and an engineer has opened a ticket saying the export is broken. What is happening?
options: The destination drops 90% of spans under load, so the team should add capacity to its collector and retry
API spans are only emitted for errors, so the missing 90% are successful requests that produced no spans
The traceparent header is malformed on most requests, so the API cannot attach spans to the right trace
This is expected: when the traceparent sampled flag is off, the API emits no spans for that request
questions.explain: The API reads trace context from the traceparent header, and when the sampled flag is off it does not emit the request's span or the spans under it. With 10% head sampling, about 90% of requests are unsampled by design. If the team needs more API spans, it must change its own sampling decision. Collector overload is the near-miss: delivery is best effort and spans can be lost, but a steady 90% matches the sampling rate, not random loss. Spans are not limited to errors, and nothing indicates malformed headers.
questions.constraint: 10% head sampling; about 90% of requests have no API spans
breaks: a loss rate that exactly matches the sampling rate is not collector overload
API spans are emitted for successful requests as well
nothing indicates malformed headers; the rate matches sampling

questions.q: A team computes per-tenant Claude spend by summing token counts from exported API spans. Monthly totals differ from the invoice, sometimes higher and sometimes lower, by a few percent. Which TWO statements explain the gap and how to fix it? Select TWO.
options: Spans are delivered at least once, so duplicates must be removed by trace ID and span ID before summing
Span delivery is best effort and lost spans are not resent, so billing should reconcile from the Usage and Cost API
Metadata-only mode leaves token counts out of spans, so the totals are estimated from timing and are inaccurate
Spans are emitted only for sampled requests, so the totals should be multiplied by the inverse sampling rate before billing
The API double-counts cached tokens in spans, so cache read tokens should be subtracted from each span's input
questions.explain: Delivery is at least once, which inflates sums unless duplicates are removed by trace and span ID, and it is best effort, so lost spans are never resent and deflate sums. Spans suit attribution and debugging; billing should reconcile against the Usage and Cost API. Scaling by the sampling rate is the near-miss: it fits sampled traces, but it adds an estimate to a billing figure and does not explain totals that are sometimes too high. Metadata-only spans do carry token counts, and nothing supports cache double-counting.
questions.constraint: span-based totals are sometimes above and sometimes below the invoice
breaks: metadata-only spans still include token counts
scaling estimates billing and cannot explain totals that run high
no evidence that spans double-count cached tokens
