questions.domain: Agent Fleet Operations for Software Delivery
questions.q: A CI fleet launches about 300 claude -p --worktree jobs a day to fix flaky tests in parallel. After two weeks, build machines run out of disk, and new jobs fail because their worktree names are already locked. What should the jobs do?
options: Run every job in the main checkout instead, since worktrees are only useful for interactive sessions
Remove each job's worktree in a cleanup step, because non-interactive runs do not clean them up
Raise cleanupPeriodDays so that the periodic sweep keeps worktrees for longer before removing any of them
Give every job a random worktree name, so locked names do not collide, and add more disk to each machine
questions.explain: Non-interactive runs with -p have no exit prompt, so Claude does not clean up their worktrees and leaves each creation lock in place until a later stale-lock sweep. At 300 jobs a day, worktrees and locks pile up. An explicit cleanup step in each job fixes it. Random names are the near-miss: they avoid the lock collisions, but the worktrees still accumulate until disks fill again. The main checkout loses isolation between parallel jobs, and a longer retention period makes the pile-up worse.
questions.constraint: -p runs leave their worktrees and locks behind
breaks: parallel jobs in one checkout lose isolation and collide
longer retention makes the accumulation worse
avoids name collisions but worktrees still pile up

questions.domain: Agent Fleet Operations for Software Delivery
questions.q: A lead runs an agent team of five teammates to add a feature across a service. Afterwards, two teammates' changes to the shared config module are missing, and the transcripts show both edited that module. How should the lead structure the next run?
options: Add more teammates so that the work finishes faster and there is less time for overlapping edits
Split the work so each teammate owns a separate set of files, with the shared module owned by one
Ask all teammates to re-read the config module before saving, so that each sees the latest version
Have every teammate write its changes to the module at the very end, after all the other work is done
questions.explain: Teammates work independently, and two teammates editing the same file leads to overwrites. Decomposing the work so that each owns separate files, with any shared module owned by a single teammate who takes requests from the others, removes the race. Re-reading before saving is the near-miss: it narrows the window but leaves a read-modify-write race between independent writers. More teammates add coordination overhead and conflicts, and deferring the edits to the end concentrates them into the same race.
questions.constraint: two independent teammates edited the same file
breaks: more teammates mean more coordination overhead and more conflicts
narrows the window but leaves a read-modify-write race
deferring the edits concentrates them into the same race

questions.q: A platform team exports Claude Code telemetry from 600 engineers. They want to find which kinds of request lead to the longest chains of tool calls and API errors, across the whole fleet rather than in one session. How should they aggregate the events?
options: Group events by prompt.id, so each user prompt's tool decisions, API requests and errors roll up together
Group events by session ID only, and then sort the sessions by their total duration across the fleet to find the worst
Sample one full session per engineer each week, and read each one to judge which requests went badly for that engineer
Count total tool calls per engineer each day, and investigate the engineers with the highest totals
questions.explain: prompt.id links every event produced while processing a single user prompt, so grouping by it yields one unit per request, with its tool calls, API requests and errors. That is the right grain for finding which kinds of request produce long chains. Grouping by session is the near-miss: it works for whole-session questions, but a session mixes many prompts, so long chains are blurred together. Hand-reading samples does not scale to 600 engineers, and per-engineer totals measure people, not request types.
questions.constraint: the analysis is per request type across the fleet
breaks: a session mixes many prompts, so per-request chains are blurred
hand-reading samples does not scale and is not an aggregate
per-engineer totals measure people, not kinds of request

questions.domain: Agent Fleet Operations for Software Delivery
questions.q: An engineering org turned on Claude Code Review and wants to start blocking merges on its findings within a month, because human review cannot keep up with agent-generated pull requests. Which plan fits?
options: Make the Code Review check required in branch protection now, so its findings block merges from today
Run it in shadow, compare findings with human reviews, then gate via Approvals in observe mode first
Replace human review with Code Review on all repositories at once, since it already filters false positives
Keep Code Review advisory permanently, since automated review findings should not influence merge decisions
questions.explain: A review on its own does not approve or block a pull request, and its check run does not conclude as a failure, so it needs calibration before it gates anything. Running it in shadow, measuring its findings against human reviews, and then trialling a policy in Claude Approvals' observe mode shows what the gate would decide before it is enforced. Making the check required is the near-miss: it moves fast, but it hands gating authority to an uncalibrated instrument. Replacing humans everywhere skips calibration entirely, and ruling out gating forever ignores the review bottleneck.
questions.constraint: gating within a month, but the reviewer is not yet calibrated against humans
breaks: grants gating authority before any calibration against human review
skips calibration and removes human oversight at once
ignores the review bottleneck the org must solve

questions.domain: Agent Fleet Operations for Software Delivery
questions.q: A security engineer worries that a malicious pull request could add a REVIEW.md telling Claude Code Review to ignore the injected backdoor in the same PR. What is the accurate assessment?
options: The risk is real, so REVIEW.md should be deleted from every repository and the review instructions kept in a wiki outside the code
Review instructions come from the base or default branch, never the PR's own changes, so this PR cannot redirect them
The risk is real, so every PR that touches REVIEW.md must be blocked automatically by a separate CI job
Claude ignores REVIEW.md for security findings anyway, so whatever a PR adds to the file has no effect
questions.explain: Code Review reads REVIEW.md from the base or default branch and never from the pull request's own changes, so a PR cannot rewrite the instructions used to review it. Changes to REVIEW.md still deserve normal review before they merge, since they will apply to later PRs. Blocking every PR that touches the file is the near-miss: it feels safe, but the attack it targets is already prevented, and it adds friction to legitimate edits. Deleting the file loses tuning, and there is no documented special-casing of security findings.
questions.constraint: the instructions come from the base branch, not from the PR
breaks: drops useful tuning to defend against an attack already prevented
targets an attack the instruction source already prevents
no documented exemption for security findings

questions.domain: Agent Fleet Operations for Software Delivery
questions.q: Agents now open three times as many pull requests as a year ago, and reviewers approve most of them within minutes. A sample audit found that reviewers rarely ran the code or read the tests. Which oversight change best restores real verification?
options: Require two human approvals on every agent pull request, regardless of what it changes
Require agents to attach evidence (tests, run output, screenshots), and route risky paths to deeper review
Ban agent-generated pull requests on Fridays, so reviewers have one day a week to catch up on the queue of open requests
Ask reviewers to sign a statement that they ran the code, recorded as a checkbox in each pull request before merge
questions.explain: When generation outpaces review, the fix is to make verification cheap and focus scarce attention: agents attach evidence that the change works, and review depth scales with risk so humans spend time where mistakes cost most. Two approvals everywhere is the near-miss: it adds people, but the audit shows reviewers are already skimming, so doubling skims on every change just spreads the same attention thinner. A Friday ban shifts the queue, and a checkbox records a claim, not verification.
questions.constraint: review volume tripled and reviewers no longer verify changes
breaks: doubles skimmed approvals without making verification cheaper
moves the queue around instead of improving verification
a checkbox records a claim, not actual verification

questions.q: A developer set up a nightly dependency audit with /loop in a Claude Code session on their laptop. It runs some nights and silently skips others, always on nights the laptop was asleep or Claude Code was closed. What should they use instead?
options: Keep /loop, but shorten the interval to every hour so that at least one run lands during each night
A cloud scheduled task with a nightly schedule trigger, which runs even when the laptop is closed
Keep /loop, but resume the session each morning with --resume so the missed runs are caught up
A cron job on the laptop that starts claude -p each night, with power-saving turned off permanently
questions.explain: Session-scoped tasks only fire while Claude Code is running and idle, with no catch-up for missed fires. A cloud scheduled task runs on Anthropic-managed or self-hosted infrastructure, so it keeps working when the laptop is closed. Resuming with --resume is the near-miss: it restores unexpired tasks, but missed fires are not caught up. A shorter interval still needs the laptop awake, and a laptop cron job depends on the same machine.
questions.constraint: the job must run nightly whether or not the laptop is on
breaks: still runs only while the laptop and session are up
resuming restores tasks but does not catch up missed fires
still depends on the laptop being on every night

questions.q: An engineer starts /goal with the condition 'the staging deploy is healthy', and Claude keeps working, then declares success while staging is still failing. The evaluator's verdict says the condition appeared to be met. How should the condition be written?
options: Make the condition stricter in wording, such as 'the staging deploy is fully and completely healthy'
Name evidence Claude's output can show, such as 'the health check prints 200 for all five services'
Add a Stop hook that blocks Claude from ending a turn, so the goal cannot be marked complete early
Raise the session's effort level so the evaluator inspects staging more thoroughly before it decides
questions.explain: The /goal evaluator judges the condition against what Claude has surfaced in the conversation; it does not run commands or read files itself. A vague condition can look satisfied from Claude's narrative, so the condition should name evidence that appears in the transcript, such as a health-check command's output. Stricter wording is the near-miss: it sounds more demanding, but the evaluator still has nothing concrete to check. A Stop hook that blocks every stop never lets the goal end, and effort does not let the evaluator inspect staging.
questions.constraint: the evaluator reads only what Claude's output shows
breaks: stricter words still give the evaluator nothing concrete to check
blocking every stop means the goal can never end
the evaluator does not inspect systems, whatever the effort

questions.q: A company publishes a list of approved MCP servers to its Claude Code fleet in managed allowedMcpServers. An audit finds engineers using unapproved servers, because they added them to their own user settings. Security wants the list to be the whole set. What should change?
options: Move the list from managed settings into each repository's .mcp.json file so that it ships with the code
Also set allowManagedMcpServersOnly to true, so the managed list cannot be broadened by users
Add every unapproved server the audit found to deniedMcpServers, and repeat the audit every month
Ask engineers to remove unapproved servers, with a reminder in the onboarding guide and in CLAUDE.md
questions.explain: allowedMcpServers on its own is a soft allowlist that users can broaden in their own settings. Adding allowManagedMcpServersOnly turns it into an approved catalogue: users can add servers from the list, and anything else is blocked. Denylisting known servers is the near-miss: it blocks the ones the audit found, but every new unapproved server is allowed until the next audit. A repository .mcp.json is not a policy, and reminders are not enforcement.
questions.constraint: the managed list must be the complete set; users currently broaden it
breaks: a repository file is not a policy that blocks other servers
blocks only known servers; new unapproved ones still load
reminders do not enforce anything

questions.q: A company is rolling Claude Code out to 900 engineers. Requirements: all model traffic must go through the company's LLM gateway, and the same policy must apply when engineers run cloud sessions in Anthropic-hosted environments. Devices are managed through MDM. Which TWO configuration steps meet both requirements? Select TWO.
options: In managed settings, set allowedProviders to customEndpoint and put the gateway's ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL in the env block
Configure server-managed settings as well, because endpoint-managed settings do not reach cloud sessions
Ask every engineer to export ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL in their shell profile, with a check in the onboarding script that verifies the variable is set correctly
Put ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL in each repository's .claude/settings.json, so that every clone routes to the gateway
Block api.anthropic.com on the office firewall, so that sessions can only reach the model through the gateway
questions.explain: Setting allowedProviders to customEndpoint with the gateway's ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL in the same managed file makes the gateway the only destination Claude Code accepts. MDM-delivered, endpoint-managed settings do not reach cloud sessions in Anthropic-hosted environments, so server-managed settings must carry the policy there too. The firewall rule is the near-miss: it blocks direct traffic from the office, but not from home networks or cloud sessions, and it leaves the setting unenforced in Claude Code itself. Shell exports and repository settings can be changed or skipped by users.
questions.constraint: gateway-only routing, enforced on devices and in Anthropic-hosted cloud sessions
breaks: a user-level export can be changed or skipped
a repository setting can be overridden and is not organisational policy
covers only the office network, not home or cloud sessions
